content_voiceover: This flowchart shows how to manage ICANS once you've assigned a grade. For grade one, close monitoring is sufficient, along with workup such as EEG, MRI, and lumbar puncture to rule out other causes. From grade two onward, you notify the ICU and involve neurology, consider holding oral intake and switching medications to intravenous formulations, and for grade three and four you should strongly consider ICU transfer. Across grades two through four, in the absence of contraindications, pursue EEG, MRI, and lumbar puncture for differential diagnosis. Outside of clinical trials, ICANS specific therapies remain limited. One key pearl here, when grade one CRS occurs together with grade two or higher ICANS, steroids rather than tocilizumab are the appropriate treatment, though that approach is not suitable for more severe CRS. If seizures occur, clinically or on EEG, give levetiracetam and benzodiazepines, and if seizures persist or recur, repeat benzodiazepines, otherwise treat as status epilepticus. Standard therapy is intravenous dexamethasone ten milligrams every six hours for one to three days. If there is cerebral edema, consider hyperosmolar therapy. If the patient worsens, escalate to intravenous methylprednisolone, one thousand milligrams a day for three days, then tapering down through two hundred fifty, one hundred twenty five, and sixty milligrams twice daily. For truly refractory ICANS, discuss alternative therapies such as anakinra, an anti IL one receptor agent, siltuximab, an anti IL six agent, or intrathecal or systemic chemotherapy.
keypoints: Grade two and up triggers ICU notification and neurology consult
Grade one CRS plus grade two or higher ICANS calls for steroids, not tocilizumab
Seizures are treated with levetiracetam and benzodiazepines
First line is IV dexamethasone, escalating to high dose methylprednisolone if refractory
Refractory cases may need anakinra, siltuximab, or intrathecal chemotherapy
